#1007. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

“We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which showed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

#997. Daily briefing: Older people are staying sharp for longer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty

People entering their golden years now have better memory and experience slower cognitive decline than previous generations. A study of people born between 1910 and 1964 found that a ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Researchers speculate that improvements in memory might be thanks to better education, health care and nutrition in childhood, while the slower decline in cognitive function might be influenced by factors later in life, such as improved treatment for cardiovascular and metabolic disease.

The large language models that underlie chatbots such as ChatGPT are quickly overcoming some of their weaknesses, say computer scientists Owen Queen and James Zou. They analysed flaws — such as hallucinating references — that had been flagged by researchers in academic papers. Most flaws were no longer a problem within roughly 16 months of a paper’s publication — for example, the latest models hardly ever attribute information to sources that don’t exist. On the other hand, newer models are getting more sycophantic and worse at generating random numbers.

Reference: Owen Queen & James Zou blog post

Undergraduate students were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging variants of the SARS-CoV-2 virus between 2021 and 2023, according to a massive genetic analysis. Researchers found that viral transmission during that period was highest among school students between the ages of 15 and 18, university undergrads and nursing-home residents. However, staff at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. The study’s scale “is truly impressive”, says infectious-disease researcher Bill Hanage.

A report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) suggests that science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, and standards for doing so are applied inconsistently across journals. NASEM recommends that the editorial review process be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months. The report was due to be published on 19 November, but was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained references with fabricated author names, which could suggest that artificial intelligence was used to draft or edit it.

Earlier this week we tried our hands at a game that tests our ability to decode ‘tortured phrases’ — ridiculous synonyms for common terms, which are intended to obscure plagiarism. For example, instead of ‘big data’, a study might use ‘colossal information’. The quiz inspired Briefing reader Chris Schneider to suggest her own tongue-in-cheek tortured phrase for our own dear ‘Nature Briefing’: “Essence of donning underwear.”

In the spirit of silliness, we’d like to hear your best science-related tortured phrases — whether spotted in the wild or invented just for fun. Entertain us at briefing@nature.com

Bees are the well-deserved superstars of the pollination world, and the reputations of birds, bats and even wasps are on the rise. Make room, now, for flies. Diptera — especially hoverflies (Syrphidae) — are undervalued pollinators. For example, on strawberry farms in England, hoverflies can make up more than half of the pollinating insects. Meanwhile, our reliance on managed honeybees can actually damage biodiversity and crop quality.

The New Yorker | 16 min read (intermittent paywall)

An artificially intelligent human wants to make choices that matter in The right to do wrong.

For the first time, astrophysicists have directly observed a giant star — one that’s swelling in size toward the end of its life cycle — engulfing a nearby ‘companion’ star in its gas envelope. Now they wait to learn what comes next. The companion star could cause the giant star to shed its gas envelope, after which the two could settle into a tight orbit; or it could plunge into the giant star’s core to its doom. “To conclusively rule out either case, we need to continue observing the system,” says astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar.

Space physicist Emma Bunce has been working on the European–Japanese BepiColombo mission for 20 years. After an eight-year journey battling the Sun's immense gravitational pull, if all goes well, it will finally enter Mercury’s orbit tomorrow. (The Guardian | 3 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03816-3

Today Leif Penguinson is visiting Lushan Geopark in Jiujiang, China. Can you find the penguin?

The answer will be in Monday’s e-mail, all thanks to Briefing photo editor and penguin wrangler Tom Houghton.

#996. Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia

International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's world championship.

A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

#995. Kevin De Bruyne insists potential punishment over Man City's guilty verdict will not tarnish his old club's achievements under Pep Guardiola - or diminish his 'love' for the owners

Published: 16:01 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:04 EST, 23 November 2026

Manchester City legend Kevin De Bruyne insisted that any potential punishment for breaching financial rules will not change what Pep Guardiola’s team achieved and their memories of success.

The Belgian was a key pillar during the spell of unprecedented domestic dominance and has a statue commissioned outside the Etihad Stadium.

De Bruyne is back in town with Napoli for Tuesday’s Champions League tie, reiterating his ‘love’ for City and its owners, while revealing recent talks with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.

The 35-year-old brushed off suggestions that silverware collected during his decade at City would be tarnished if the club lost their appeal and were sanctioned after being found guilty of the vast majority of charges levelled at them.

De Bruyne’s trophy haul – six Premier League titles, one Champions League, two FA Cups and five Carabao Cups – were largely secured outside of the nine-year period in which City were scrutinised, up to 2018.

‘I’m proud of what I've done as a football player,’ De Bruyne said. ‘Honestly, this is my club, I love the owners. I've talked about a lot of stuff outside football (with them), I've even spoken to Khaldoon about how to buy a club and everything.

The 36-year-old brushed off suggestions that silverware collected during his decade at City would be tarnished if the club lost their appeal

‘It (stripping of titles) still doesn't change (anything), my football has not changed. I don't think a lot of people will change in their mind how they view me as a player, or how we played.

‘But everybody has his own opinion and other people may be disgraced a bit. I can't change anything about that.’

De Bruyne’s final two seasons at City were plagued by injury before he joined Napoli on a free transfer in 2025 and his first return in last year’s Champions League lasted just 26 minutes as he hobbled off.

Classed as the greatest player in the club’s modern history, De Bruyne was typically forthright on the uncertainty surrounding his former employers after the guilty verdicts read by a three-person independent commission.

‘My feelings have never been different,’ he added. ‘Honestly, the way that I feel is just the way that I've been treated by this club, what I've done with this club for me personally, and how we've worked together as a group.

‘Of course, it's a lot of things that have been going on. I have nothing but affection for this club, and that will never change. Even now, the people who treated me and my family for 10 years is the most important thing.’

De Bruyne left City under duress, vehemently disagreeing with the club’s decision not to offer him a new contract following a spate of injuries before choosing Napoli – and his long-term future in Serie A is now appearing in doubt.

All eyes in Italy were on the midfielder’s public response to an interview published with his wife, Michele, in which she was reported to have criticised life in Naples and yearned for a move away. Those comments were taken out of context, according to a visibly frustrated De Bruyne, with PSV Eindhoven looking at securing a transfer in January.

De Bruyne left City under duress but revealed recent talks with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak

But City supporters will have been more interested in how far De Bruyne went in backing their club ahead of next month’s appeal hearing.

‘In life there are rules, but everybody plays to the limit, I would say,’ he claimed, seemingly referring to how financial rules are interpreted by the Premier League’s elite clubs.

‘I played in between the white lines, and I competed with other players, and I had many experiences with my teams.

#991. As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?

Droughts, floods and extreme heat are upping the pressure on delegates at the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey. Can countries move beyond pledges to concrete action?

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet."

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff."

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to agree, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels."

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements, including phaseout plans.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.

The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.

"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power which Germany and other industrialized nations rely on to shape policy to fight climate change.

Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.

When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

This article was originally written in German.

Former Manchester United midfielder Paul Scholes has become the latest ex-Red Devil to tear into the club's defence, criticising Leny Yoro following his red card in his side's 4-0 defeat by Liverpool.

He added: 'You know what, he’s come in to a really bad setup defensively now. I think they also made the point yesterday if he went in next to (Virgil) Van Dijk he might look a little bit better but he doesn’t look Premier League level. He looks like a rabbit in the headlights.'

Paul Scholes (pictured) has suggested Leny Yoro is not yet ready for the Premier League

Yoro was sent off in the opening minutes of Manchester United's 4-0 defeat by Liverpool

Fellow former United midfielder Nicky Butt, who played alongside Scholes for United between 1994 and 2004, added: 'If that’s Man United in our day, he’s on loan like a Jonny Evans or a John O’Shea. He’s a great talent that will come good.'

Scholes, though, wasn't having any of it.

He replied: 'I’m not sure how much of a great talent he is. I think he has shown a little bit of a sign in the France squad but every time I’ve seen him he doesn’t look at the races. Everything’s happening around him and he’s just a bit, oh, what do I do?'

United have also faced criticism for their apparent lack of running this season, with eyebrows raised when Youri Tielemans said in the summer that they didn't do much prior to the campaign getting under way.

That, according to Butt, is down to the players.

'We’ve had our say about the players and they’re just not good enough,' he said. 'It is the most unathletic team I’ve ever seen in Man United.

'I’m going to go through a team and I’m trying to be as honest as I can. Forget the quality for right now. For me, physicality-wise, if you go through a team, the right back, he’s physically OK, but he’s not amazing. De Ligt or Harry, whoever he’s going to play in there, physically not great. Martinez for me is physically not great. You got Yoro who will physically come good.

Nicky Butt (pictured), meanwhile, has criticised the physical ability of many of United's players

'Then I go on to the midfield, none of them are physically good enough. Kobbie can get about the pitch 15-20 yards, but he’s not box to box. Said that numerous times. He’s got a lot of talent. He’s got a lot of things going for him. I think he’s a top player. He ain’t got the legs. He needs to have legs around him but his legs around him at the minute are Bruno and Tielemans - and they can’t run around.

'Look at Mbeumo, I think he’s OK but he’s not going to blow anybody away. I think Cunha can run. So then you look at the whole squad and you’re saying three players can run.

'What I’m getting at there, and it sounds like I’m being a draconian but what you have to do first and foremost when you go to Anfield is to be able to compete physically and they can’t so they have no chance.'

Greenwood has been Fenerbahce’s best player by far tonight and he tests Alisson. Lukaku finds Greenwood with a pass forward down the left channel and, from inside the Liverpool penalty area, the latter forces Alisson into a decent save.

What started off as an encouraging performance has descended into something ordinary at best for Liverpool. They are being overrun in midfield and the pace of Greenwood down Fenerbahce’s right has the beating of Kostas Tsimikas on every occasion. Andoni Iraola will be delighted to get in for half-time all square - if Liverpool can see it out.

Greenwood has an opportunity from the right side of the box. He tries to beat Alisson at his near post but drags it wide.

Munoz’s cross from near the byline is met by Barcola and the Frenchman’s header goes narrowly wide of the far post.

Tsimikas’ inswinging corner from the right is put into a dangerous area and Skriniar’s header goes over his own bar for another on the other side. Szoboszlai feeds one in towards the near post and Lukaku heads away.

Mason Greenwood is having his name bellowed around the stadium though the deflection off Jeremy Jacquet is the only reason he has scored. Emotions are running high in the stadium, especially in the press box which seems to be an overspill for home supporters. One of Trey Nyoni’s former coaches has an observer’s seat here and he cheered why Nyoni scored. Greenwood’s leveller saw those who had taken umbrage at something so inoffensive return the cheering ten-fold with some pretty colourful gestures, too.

The hosts are back on level terms. Fenerbahce have a free-kick not far outside the Liverpool penalty area, one that should never have been given after Szoboszlai is penalised for a foul on Kante that was not a foul. Greenwood steps up to take and his free-kick takes a huge deflection off Jacquet. That deflection takes it away from Alisson and into the Liverpool net. Alisson is not impressed with his wall.

Fenerbahce are inches away from equalising moments after going behind as they hit the frame of the goal. Brown’s cross from the left side of the box finds Kahveci, whose shot comes back off the bar. It would have been a very close call with offside had the ball gone in.

The visitors take the lead in Istanbul and it is 19-year-old Nyoni who scores. A cross from Szoboszlai into the Fenerbahce penalty area is headed out to the edge of the box, where Nyoni volleys it first time. The shot takes a small deflection off Oppong and beats Ederson.

What a moment for Trey Nyoni 🥹 The young Liverpool midfielder scores his first professional goal, and he does it on the Champions League stage ✨ 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Vtj4Yd3tnn

Fenerbahce want a penalty. The ball is played in behind the Liverpool defence and Greenwood takes a sensational first touch. Tsimikas races back and there is a small push on Greenwood, who goes down. The referee waves the appeals away and the VAR clears the incident.

Should Barcola have done better there? Ngumoha finds Gomez in acres of space out on the right. Gomez then first time delivers a very dangerous cross right through the corridor of uncertainty looking for Barcola but the Frenchman cannot connect.

Munoz wins Liverpool a corner out on the right after Yuksek blocked the cross from the Spaniard. Szoboszlai’s outswinger is headed away at the near post by Yuksek, who has made two good defensive actions in a matter of moments.

Liverpool have so much more quality on the ball when they keep possession but the final ball - especially from the left hand side - is letting them down at the moment. They are making light of a sodden pitch and some overzealous attempts by Fenerbahce to disrupt them. The first 15 minutes has been played out primarily to a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling but, looking at those fans around us, none of them are getting involved. Could it be the whistles are being piped in on a pre-recorded file?

Szoboszlai hits the free-kick but ends up hitting his own man. The effort did appear to be going on target but Munoz got in the way. Liverpool’s plan to set up a mini wall of their own to block out the view of Ederson backfired.

Ngumoha shows great footwork to skip past a few Fenerbahce defenders before Kante barges right into the back of the English teenager to give Liverpool a free-kick not far outside the Fenerbahce penalty area.

Liverpool have dominated possession in these early stages and have settled into the game well. Fenerbahce may not be in the best of form but this is still a tricky away trip.

Liverpool come close to the opening goal of the game. Tsimikas’ cross from the left comes all the way to the back post, where Munoz hits it. The Spaniard scuffs his effort and the ball comes to Barcola, who also scuffs his shot. The ball comes back to Munoz, whose powerful shot is parried behind by Ederson for a corner.

Fenerbahce deal with the initial delivery but Liverpool keep it alive. Szoboszlai sends in a dangerous delivery, which Jacquet meets, but the Frenchman’s header from six yards out goes wide. Jacquet should have done better with that chance.

Before we get going, we pause to pay tribute to Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died the other day.

We are under way in Istanbul, with the weather similar tonight in Turkey as to what it was like in Barcelona last night. Can Liverpool make it four wins from four in this season’s Champions League?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel into the pouring rain and we are moments away from kick-off in Istanbul. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

So many of Fenerbahce’s team were Premier League regulars, which begged the question - is this a team with more English top-flight experience than Liverpool? The answer is here: Liverpool’s starting line-up has 1241 Premier League appearances. Fenerbahce have 1086.

“I think we have been [rotating] basically all the season. You play every three, four days you have to refresh the legs. The defensive positions we do not have as many options. We have injuries but offensively I think we can rotate a little bit and today we can see other players.”

On Bradley Barcola playing as a central striker:

“I think Bradley, even Victor [Munoz], are players that are wingers but have played sometimes up front. I think we should be mobile. I think we should attack the spaces that are there. The Hungarian has been struggling of late with a hamstring injury but, having returned to the matchday squad on Sunday against Arsenal, he is now back into the starting XI tonight.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

#983. 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner said. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

"For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he said.

Eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."

Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

"I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color."

She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

#981. Man United's January transfer budget will be less than £50m with Mauricio Pochettino expected to make only TWO signings - despite needing to bolster their attack and defence

Published: 16:30 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:03 EST, 23 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino will have less than £50million to buy Manchester United out of trouble in the January transfer window.

Pochettino admitted that United are in a relegation battle after a painful 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in his first game in charge left the club second from bottom of the Premier League.

It’s understood the Argentine will have a limited budget well under £50million with United’s hands tied by the league’s new financial rules. Pochettino is only expected to make two new signings in January, even if one of them is a loan deal.

Sources have not ruled out the possibility of United gambling if there is a genuine threat of the club being relegated for the first time in 53 years, but they would still have to spend responsibly.

The defeat to Liverpool underlined the need for Pochettino to strengthen in central defence, with Brentford’s Nathan Collins emerging as a strong candidate ahead of Calvin Bassey, who is expected to sign a new contract with Fulham, and Everton’s Jarrad Branthwaite who is valued at over £70million.

United also want a left-back after failing to sign cover for Luke Shaw in the summer when they were linked with Barcelona’s Alejandro Balde and Rayan Ait-Nouri of Manchester City. Both those players could be potential targets again.

Mauricio Pochettino will have less than £50million to try and fix Manchester United in January

Pochettino is only expected to make two new signings in January - pictured: Chief executive Omar Berrada (left) and director of football Jason Wilcox (centre)

Pochettino would also like a new striker after Benjamin Sesko’s shin injury left him short of firepower until the New Year.

Monaco’s Folarin Balogun, who played under Pochettino for the US national team, Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Ivan Toney, the former Brentford centre-forward now playing for Al-Ahli, have all been linked with a move to Old Trafford.

However, Toney’s £500,000-a-week wages put him out of United’s reach, and Leeds are keen to extend Calvert-Lewin’s contract which is worth £180,000-a-week.

Meanwhile, United are appealing to the FA over Leny Yoro’s controversial red card against Liverpool.

Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute at Anfield for a challenge on Alexander Isak on the edge of the penalty box. The Frenchman was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott, and Dominik Szoboszlai scored Liverpool’s first goal from the free-kick.

However, United insist that Yoro did not deny Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity because goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have reached the ball first.

The club have notified the FA of their intention to appeal in the hope of having Yoro’s one-match ban overturned so he can play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

#975. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

Leipzig are guilty of overelaboration in and around the City box. Too many tricks and flicks, not enough shots and crosses. Haaland is giving his team-mates some jip for not reading his runs.

Cherki pings a pass out to Enzo on the right and he slips as he tries to cross, his momentum as he fell forcing the cross deeper than he had planned and it sails beyond a visibly frustrated Haaland who keeps making good runs but has yet to be found.

City are dicing with danger by letting Nusa run at them from positions on both wings and through the middle. They manage to stop him threading ir flicking passes through to Romulo twice in the space of 30 seconds but it would be less stressful to cut it off at source further away from their goal.

A replay of Donnarumma’s ‘save’ show that it was on target and the keeper could easily have squirted it through his hands into the goal. Small wonder he rotated his head as if auditioning for a part in the Exorcist to look back in relief.

Leipzig take the corner short and City push them back and try to start a counter that ends when Baumgartner takes Anderson out with a rash sliding tackle that upends the England midfielder.

Ndiaye rides his luck and two tackles before the ball just skips away form him as he was closing towards the 18-yard line but Leipzig botch the clearance and Foden feeds a lovely pass in from the right to Cherki who opens his body and wraps a left-foot shot the wrong side of the left post.

Cherki intercepts a pass meant for Nusa but goes backwards instead of looking for Foden down the right, killing the impetus of an unexpected interception.

Nusa stretches his legs down the left after a clumsy lay-off from Cherki and shifts the ball inside to meet Romulo’s run between Khusanov and Nunes but Nunes sticks with him and forces him deep, so close to the byline in fact that his attempt to square it goes straight to Donnarumma.

Khusanov, under pressure from Romulo, squeezes a pass that deflects off him and goes out for a City throw-in.

After a moment’s silence for Jesús de Miguel who was killed after being injured while playing for Tenerife earlier this week, Manchester City kick off, attacking from left to right. They are in black with yellow trim, the colours of the bee emblem of the city of Manchester. Leipzig are in white with red bits. City only have a small portion of the stadium for travelling support – but the boos for the Champions League anthem is heard loud and clear. There are a few fans dressed up as sheikhs too.

#972. The Women's World Cup is coming home... but 2035 cannot be treated as a fix for the game's problems, writes TARA ANSON-WALSH

Published: 14:36 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:04 EST, 23 November 2026

The United Kingdom will host the 2035 Women's World Cup, the first football World Cup to be staged on these shores since 1966, it was announced to much fanfare on Monday.

Yet while the countdown can now officially begin, the biggest challenges facing the women's game cannot be kicked eight-and-a-half years down the road.

Over in Zurich, FIFA president Gianni Infantino undertook his usual long-winded and self-serving monologue which precedes these ceremonies, in which he heralded the 'incredible growth' of the Women's World Cup, describing a time when they 'didn't exist'.

'We all remember the last Women's World Cup,' the embattled 56-year-old Italian said, calling it 'a huge success'.

The irony, of course, is that the last Women's World Cup in Australia and New Zealand is remembered by many for all the wrong reasons, with newspaper back pages peppered with images of Spain captain Jenni Hermoso's kiss with the former president of Spain's FA, Luis Rubiales, for days after the final.

Rubiales was later convicted of sexual assault for the incident, which triggered widespread protests across the country and overshadowed Spain's terrific 1-0 triumph over England in Sydney.

Gianni Infantino undertook his usual long-winded and self-serving monologue which precedes these ceremonies, in which he heralded the 'incredible growth' of the Women's World Cup

Rubiales was later convicted of sexual assault for the incident, which triggered widespread protests across the country and overshadowed Spain's terrific 1-0 triumph over England

There is an added layer of irony in that Infantino had, two days before the 2023 final, angered many women worldwide with yet another controversial speech in which he told them: 'You have the power to change', but that they had to 'convince us men what we have to do'.

Alongside this patronising statement, Infantino also insisted that equal pay at the World Cup 'would not solve anything'.

Three years later, Infantino is unfortunately still at the helm, while UEFA's attempts to unseat him following his controversial bid to sell off the World Cup now look to have failed spectacularly, with the football despot increasingly likely to secure a fourth term.

What the social and political landscape will look like by the time this women's footballing bonanza arrives on these shores in 2035 remains unclear. What is clear, however, is that the game's continued progress will require more than the record attendances and soaring commercial revenues the FA are predicting.

It will require the figures who have too often held it back to finally step aside, and that process should begin with the likes of Infantino being shown the door.

It will require those at the top of English football to put their heads together and work out how to stem falling attendances in the league. The average attendance across the first eight WSL matchweeks of 2024-25 was 8,173. Last season it was 7,472. This season, it is tracking at around 5,677.

And third, it will require somewhere other than Wembley to stage the final.

Wembley was, of course, the scene of Chloe Kelly's moment of madness, yet by the time the 2035 Women's World Cup comes around it will also have hosted the men's finals of Euro 2024 and 2028.

The FA paid off its debt on the national stadium in 2024, 17 years after its reopening, and is no longer obligated to host major events there to service repayments.

The rules have been left open for another venue to emerge to host the final, such as Man United's proposed new 100,000 stadium

While under current FIFA regulations, Wembley is the only one of the proposed 22 stadiums that meets the requirements to host a final, the rules have been left open enough for another venue to emerge should a suitable stadium be completed before 2035.

Step up Sir Jim Ratcliffe, although please refer back to point one in this regard – the Manchester United co-owner who famously asked former captain Katie Zelem 'what do you do here?' while touring the club's women's facilities.

United's proposed new 100,000-seater stadium was included in the 2035 bid and could yet come under consideration from FIFA.

While there are still many hurdles to clear before then, hosting a tournament final in Manchester would undoubtedly be huge for the women's game, not least given the optics of a bid built around being 'all together', described as 'a rallying cry to unite people through football'.

London should not be the epicentre of the tournament, not if the intention is to spread the women's game across the United Kingdom rather than concentrate it in the capital, where Arsenal's attendances continue to dwarf those of every other WSL club.

In other words, the women's game in this country cannot be put on hold until 2035.

It cannot afford to wait eight-and-a-half years for this World Cup to come and rescue it. Time to get cracking.

#969. US science academy urges journals to fix errors more quickly

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J. Richards/AFP via Getty

Science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds. Standards for fixing errors are also inconsistently applied across research journals, it says.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science

There are no data on how long retraction or correction currently takes, as journals do not generally disclose when they were alerted to a problem in a paper; the NASEM report says they should. On average, according to the Retraction Watch database, retractions occur around 2.4 years after a paper is published. The report recommends that editorial review processes be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months — at least when editors are looking at concerns over a single paper.

“The big picture is, the process is too slow,” says Randy Schekman, a cell biologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who chaired the 14-person committee that produced the NASEM report. A prompter and more transparent process would strengthen the reliability of the scientific record, he says.

The report was due to be published online on 19 November, but publication was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained some references with fabricated first names for authors, a possible sign that large language models had been used to write or edit the material and had been insufficiently checked.

“It's unfortunate that there were these flawed references in a report about fixing the literature,” says Jennifer Byrne, a cancer researcher and research integrity sleuth at the University of Sydney who first flagged the concern to Science when reviewing the report, which was shared ahead of publication with media outlets.

The report had two main aims: to speed up the process of retraction or correction and to lower the “tremendous emotional barriers” for authors to correct honest mistakes in the record, Schekman says. “Part of the problem is that it’s too rare for a paper to be retracted,” he adds.

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

The report also suggests that journals shouldn’t just wait for complaints to reach them, but instead “take proactive steps” to identify errors and integrity issues. That might include journal-wide audits, or regularly monitoring social media and online platforms where post-publication issues are raised, it says.

Existing guidelines for publishers, such as those from the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in London, only urge a “timely” response to concerns without setting out expected schedules, and don’t suggest journals scan online platforms for complaints.

“A major theme running through the report is that we have to distinguish between retraction or correction, and research misconduct,” notes Dorothy Bishop, a research-integrity sleuth in Oxford, UK, who was on the NASEM committee. Authors shouldn’t associate retracting a paper with the stigma of misconduct, she says. And although journal editors sometimes wait for a university to investigate whether there is research misconduct before correcting a paper, they shouldn’t, she adds.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

Calls for changing these attitudes aren’t new: journals have long emphasized that retractions can cover honest mistakes. When it comes to journal processes, Holden Thorpe, the editor in chief of Science, urged that issuing corrections or retractions and making a determination of misconduct be separated in an editorial in 2022, and COPE guidelines already emphasize the point. But “there are still plenty of people who see a correction or retraction as an allegation of fraud,” says Thorpe, who was also on the NASEM committee. “Hopefully, this report will accelerate the recognition of the distinction,” he says.
